subtopic_detail: Investigation offered to a couple after a third consecutive first trimester loss with no living children
stem:
A 31 year old woman attends your practice with her partner two weeks after a third consecutive miscarriage, all at between seven and nine weeks. They have no living children and she conceives readily each time.

Her cycles are regular at 29 days and she has no history of pelvic infection, uterine surgery or termination. She is a non-smoker with a body mass index of 24 kg/m2 and takes no regular medication. Her thyroid function and a random glucose are normal, and her cervical screening is up to date. The couple are distressed and want to know what can be looked for before they try again.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable abdominal and pelvic examination, no adnexal mass or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, random glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), full blood count within normal limits

options.text: Test for inherited thrombophilias and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
options.rationale: Routine inherited thrombophilia screening is not recommended for recurrent first trimester loss because the association is weak and anticoagulation has not improved outcomes. The acquired antibody syndrome is a different matter. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Test for natural killer cell activity and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
options.rationale: Peripheral natural killer cell testing has no established relationship with uterine immune function and is offered mainly outside the evidence base. Acting on the result exposes women to unproven immunotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Test for antiphospholipid antibodies and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
options.rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the one cause of recurrent loss with a treatment that clearly improves live birth rates, and structural uterine anomalies are the other reliably identifiable factor. Parental karyotyping is offered selectively because a balanced translocation in a parent changes counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Test sperm DNA fragmentation and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
options.rationale: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing is not part of standard recurrent miscarriage assessment and no intervention based on it has been shown to improve live birth. It would not alter management here. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Arrange no investigations at this stage and advise trying again with reassurance about the prognosis
options.rationale: Three consecutive losses meets the threshold at which investigation is offered, and a treatable cause would otherwise be missed. Reassurance about prognosis is appropriate but accompanies rather than replaces assessment. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage is conventionally defined as three or more consecutive pregnancy losses, though investigation is often begun after two in older women or where there is another concern. The great majority of sporadic first trimester losses are caused by foetal chromosomal abnormality, and even after three losses no cause is identified in around half of couples, which is important to convey because the prognosis for a subsequent live birth remains good. The investigations that are worth doing are those attached to an intervention or to meaningful counselling: antiphospholipid antibodies, because aspirin with low molecular weight heparin improves live birth rates in confirmed cases, imaging of the uterine cavity for structural anomalies, and thyroid function. Antiphospholipid testing requires two positive results at least twelve weeks apart to confirm the diagnosis. A wide range of other tests, including inherited thrombophilia panels and immune assays, are frequently marketed to distressed couples but are not supported and can lead to unproven and potentially harmful treatment.
key_points: Three consecutive losses is the conventional threshold for investigation
No cause is found in around half of couples and the prognosis remains good
Antiphospholipid syndrome is the cause with the clearest effective treatment
Confirmation requires two positive antibody results twelve weeks apart
Inherited thrombophilia and immune panels are not part of standard assessment
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid antibodies must be positive on two occasions at least twelve weeks apart before the diagnosis is made, because transient positivity after an acute event is common and would otherwise commit a woman to unnecessary anticoagulation.

subtopic_detail: Electrolyte monitoring and supplementation in the first week of nutritional restoration for a severely underweight adolescent
stem:
A 16 year old girl is admitted under your team with anorexia nervosa. She has eaten almost nothing for eleven days and her weight has fallen to a body mass index of 13 kg/m2.

Her admission bloods show normal electrolytes including a phosphate at the lower end of the reference range. Her pulse is 42/min and she has a postural drop in blood pressure, and her electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT interval of 440 ms. The dietitian proposes commencing nutritional restoration today and asks you to write the monitoring and supplementation plan for the first week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 42/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg lying with a fall to 76/48 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 35.8 °C
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.82 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), magnesium 0.75 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), corrected QT interval 440 ms, albumin 36 g/L (35-50)
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 13 kg/m2, cool peripheries, lanugo hair, no oedema

lead_in: What monitoring and supplementation plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Daily phosphate measurement with supplementation begun once the level falls below range
options.rationale: Waiting for the level to fall means treating an established deficiency that can already have caused cardiac and respiratory compromise. The admission level offers no reassurance because the fall occurs after feeding starts. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Daily phosphate measurement with supplementation begun before the level falls below range
options.rationale: Her prolonged starvation and very low body mass index place her at high risk, and the phosphate falls only once feeding begins and insulin drives it intracellularly. Prophylactic supplementation alongside daily measurement prevents the fall rather than reacting to it. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Twice weekly phosphate measurement with supplementation begun once the level falls below range
options.rationale: This frequency will miss the rapid fall that characteristically occurs within the first seventy two hours of feeding. Monitoring interval is as important as the decision to monitor. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Delay all nutritional restoration for 72 hours while daily electrolytes are observed for stability
options.rationale: Withholding nutrition in a severely malnourished patient carries its own mortality and does not reduce the risk once feeding eventually starts. Underfeeding is now recognised as a harm in its own right. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Daily phosphate measurement with a high carbohydrate feeding regimen to restore weight rapidly
options.rationale: A high carbohydrate load is the strongest driver of the intracellular shift and would increase rather than reduce the risk. Carbohydrate content is deliberately moderated during the early phase. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the constellation of metabolic disturbances that follows the reintroduction of nutrition after a period of starvation, and hypophosphataemia is its defining feature. During starvation the body depletes intracellular phosphate, magnesium and potassium while serum levels remain deceptively normal, and when carbohydrate is reintroduced the resulting insulin surge drives these ions into cells along with glucose, producing a rapid fall in serum concentrations that can cause cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, seizures and death. Risk is stratified by body mass index, duration of minimal intake, recent weight loss and pre-existing electrolyte abnormality, and this patient is at high risk on several counts. Contemporary practice has shifted away from cautious underfeeding, which carries its own mortality, towards starting adequate nutrition while monitoring electrolytes at least daily and supplementing phosphate and thiamine prophylactically in high risk patients. Thiamine is given before or with the first feed because carbohydrate metabolism consumes it and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
key_points: Serum electrolytes are deceptively normal during starvation despite intracellular depletion
The insulin surge after carbohydrate drives phosphate into cells within days
Risk is stratified by body mass index, duration of intake and recent weight loss
Prophylactic supplementation is preferred to reacting to a fallen level
Underfeeding is itself harmful and is no longer the recommended precaution
explanation.pearls: Thiamine must be given before or alongside the first feed in a severely malnourished patient, because the carbohydrate load consumes remaining thiamine stores and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within days of starting nutrition.

sources.label: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Decision to continue resuscitation in a cardiac arrest after prolonged immersion with a core temperature of twenty six degrees
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a regional emergency department when a 24 year old man is brought in after being pulled from a mountain river. He was in the water for an estimated forty minutes before being recovered.

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started at the scene and has continued throughout a thirty minute transport. He is in cardiac arrest with a rhythm of ventricular fibrillation that has not responded to three shocks. His pupils are fixed and dilated and he is rigid, with no spontaneous respiratory effort. His oesophageal temperature reads 26 °C. There is no evidence of major trauma and no lethal injury is apparent.

data_table.Vital signs: Cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation refractory to three shocks, oesophageal temperature 26 °C, no spontaneous respiratory effort
data_table.Examination: Fixed dilated pupils, generalised rigidity, no evidence of major trauma, no obviously lethal injury
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous pH 7.18 (7.32-7.42), glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Continue resuscitation with active rewarming before any decision to stop is considered
options.rationale: Hypothermia is profoundly neuroprotective and the usual clinical signs of death, including fixed pupils and rigidity, are unreliable until the core temperature has been restored. Full neurological recovery has been documented after prolonged arrest in this setting, so resuscitation continues during rewarming. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

options.text: Cease resuscitation now, given the fixed dilated pupils and the rigidity on examination
options.rationale: These signs are produced by the hypothermia itself and cannot be interpreted at this core temperature. Applying normothermic criteria for death is the specific error this scenario tests. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

options.text: Continue resuscitation with repeated shocks and adrenaline at the standard interval throughout
options.rationale: Below about 30 °C the myocardium responds poorly to defibrillation and drug metabolism is markedly slowed, so shocks are limited and drug intervals are extended until rewarming. Standard dosing risks accumulation and toxicity. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

options.text: Cease resuscitation now, given the failure of three shocks to restore a perfusing rhythm
options.rationale: Refractoriness to defibrillation is expected at this temperature and reflects the cold myocardium rather than an unsalvageable one. Rhythm response should be reassessed as the patient warms. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

options.text: Continue resuscitation with passive external rewarming alone using blankets and a warm environment
options.rationale: Passive measures rely on the patient generating heat by shivering, which cannot occur in cardiac arrest at this temperature. Active internal rewarming is required, ideally extracorporeal. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline: Hypothermia)

explanation.summary: Accidental hypothermia with cardiac arrest is one of the few situations in which prolonged resuscitation is justified and in which the conventional signs of death cannot be applied, captured by the principle that a patient is not dead until they are warm and dead. Cooling markedly reduces cerebral metabolic demand, and intact neurological survival has been reported after several hours of cardiopulmonary resuscitation when cooling preceded the arrest. Management differs from normothermic arrest in several respects: defibrillation attempts are limited until the core temperature rises above about 30 °C because the cold myocardium responds poorly, and adrenaline is withheld or given at extended intervals because hepatic metabolism is slowed and the drug accumulates. Extracorporeal rewarming is the treatment of choice where available and produces the best survival, so early discussion with a centre offering it is important. A serum potassium above about 12 mmol/L, or an obviously lethal injury, indicates that the hypothermia followed death rather than preceded it and is one of the few grounds for stopping.
key_points: Hypothermia is neuroprotective and the signs of death are unreliable until rewarmed
Limit defibrillation attempts until the core temperature exceeds about 30 °C
Withhold or extend the interval for adrenaline because metabolism is slowed
Extracorporeal rewarming gives the best survival where it is available
A markedly raised potassium suggests death preceded the cooling
explanation.pearls: A potassium above roughly 12 mmol/L in hypothermic arrest indicates that the patient died before they cooled rather than because of the cold, and it is one of the few biochemical grounds for stopping resuscitation.

subtopic_detail: Baseline assessment required before a first stimulant prescription in an adult newly diagnosed with attention deficit disorder
stem:
A 29 year old man attends your practice having been newly diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder by a psychiatrist, who has recommended a trial of a stimulant and asked you to complete the baseline assessment.

He has lifelong difficulty sustaining attention and organising tasks, documented from school reports, and he has lost two jobs because of missed deadlines. He drinks alcohol occasionally and uses no other substances. He tells you his father died suddenly at 44 while playing sport, and that the cause was never fully explained to the family. He has no chest pain, no palpitations and no history of syncope himself.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Normal heart sounds with no murmur, no signs of heart failure, normal peripheral pulses
data_table.History: Father died suddenly at 44 during exertion with no cause established, no personal syncope, chest pain or palpitations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before starting treatment?

options.text: Record his heart rate and blood pressure and commence the stimulant at a low dose
options.rationale: Baseline observations are necessary for every patient but are insufficient here, because a normal examination does not exclude an inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy. The family history changes the threshold for investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange a urine drug screen and commence the stimulant once the result is confirmed negative
options.rationale: Substance use is worth assessing because of diversion and misuse risk, but he reports none and this does not address the cardiac question. It would not detect the risk that matters here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine instead, since it avoids any need for cardiac assessment beforehand
options.rationale: Non-stimulant agents also raise heart rate and blood pressure and do not exempt a patient from cardiac assessment where the history warrants it. Changing drug class does not resolve the concern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an electrocardiogram and cardiology assessment before the first stimulant dose
options.rationale: An unexplained sudden death in a first degree relative under fifty raises the possibility of an inherited cardiac condition and is the specific trigger for cardiac assessment rather than routine baseline observations alone. Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure, so this must be resolved before treatment begins. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange thyroid function tests and commence the stimulant once the results are within range
options.rationale: Thyroid testing is not a routine requirement before stimulant treatment and would be prompted by clinical features of thyroid disease. It does not address the inherited cardiac risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Stimulant treatment for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is effective but requires a structured baseline assessment because the drugs raise heart rate and blood pressure and are subject to misuse and diversion. Routine baseline assessment comprises pulse, blood pressure, weight, a cardiovascular history and examination, and a review of substance use and any comorbid psychiatric illness. Routine electrocardiography is not required for everyone, which makes it important to recognise the specific features that do warrant cardiac referral: a personal history of structural heart disease, exertional chest pain, palpitations or syncope, an abnormal examination, or a family history of sudden unexplained death in a first degree relative under about forty years of age. In Australia, stimulant prescribing is additionally regulated at state level with authority requirements, and ongoing monitoring includes pulse, blood pressure and weight at each dose change and periodically thereafter. Comorbid substance use disorder does not preclude treatment but influences the choice of a longer acting or less divertible preparation.
key_points: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure, so baseline observations are mandatory
Routine electrocardiography is not required for every patient
Sudden unexplained death in a young first degree relative warrants cardiac referral
Non-stimulant alternatives do not exempt a patient from cardiac assessment
State authority requirements apply to stimulant prescribing in Australia
explanation.pearls: A first degree relative who died suddenly and unexplained before about forty is the family history detail that converts a routine stimulant baseline into a cardiology referral, because inherited cardiomyopathies and channelopathies are often silent on examination.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing an expected bereavement reaction from a depressive episode five weeks after the death of a spouse
stem:
A 71 year old woman is brought to your practice by her daughter five weeks after her husband of forty six years died of pancreatic cancer. Her daughter is worried that she is depressed and asks you to start an antidepressant.

She describes waves of sadness that come when she finds his belongings or hears a particular song, interspersed with periods where she can enjoy her grandchildren's visits and laugh with them. Her sleep is broken and her appetite is reduced, and she has lost 2 kg. She says she misses him unbearably and sometimes hears his voice calling her name as she falls asleep, which she finds comforting rather than frightening. She does not blame herself for his death, retains her sense of her own worth, and says she wants to be here for her grandchildren.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband but able to be consoled and to engage warmly, no psychomotor retardation, normal cognition
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence an antidepressant now with review of her mood and tolerability in two weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants have not been shown to benefit uncomplicated grief and medicalising a normal process can undermine it. They are indicated if a depressive episode emerges. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Commence a hypnotic for the disturbed sleep with review of her mood and function in two weeks
options.rationale: Sedatives risk dependence, falls and confusion in an older person and do not address the underlying process. Broken sleep is an expected feature of early bereavement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence an antipsychotic at low dose to address the auditory experiences she has described
options.rationale: Hearing the deceased person's voice while falling asleep is a recognised and benign feature of bereavement rather than a psychotic symptom. Treating it would expose her to significant risk without benefit. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Refer urgently to the older persons mental health team for specialist assessment this week
options.rationale: Urgent specialist referral is reserved for suicidal ideation, psychotic depression, severe functional decline or failure to eat and drink, none of which is present. Her presentation can be managed in primary care with review. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Continue supportive review with practical bereavement support and no antidepressant at this stage
options.rationale: Her reactivity of mood, preserved self worth, absent suicidal ideation and comforting rather than distressing perceptual experiences are characteristic of uncomplicated grief rather than a depressive episode. Planned review allows a depressive illness to be identified if the pattern changes. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Grief and depression overlap substantially in their surface features, since sadness, tearfulness, disturbed sleep, reduced appetite and weight loss occur in both, and the distinction rests on qualitative features rather than on symptom counting. In uncomplicated grief the dysphoria comes in waves triggered by reminders, with preserved capacity for pleasure and connection between those waves, whereas depression produces a persistent and pervasive lowering of mood with global anhedonia. Self esteem is characteristically preserved in grief, while worthlessness, guilt unrelated to the death and self loathing point to depression, and fleeting perceptual experiences of the deceased person are common in bereavement and are not psychotic. Any active suicidal ideation, marked psychomotor retardation, or persistent functional collapse should prompt treatment for depression. Prolonged grief disorder is a separate diagnosis requiring persistent intense yearning and preoccupation with functional impairment beyond six to twelve months, and it responds to specific psychological therapy rather than to antidepressants.
key_points: Grief produces waves of dysphoria with preserved reactivity between them
Depression produces persistent pervasive low mood with global anhedonia
Preserved self worth favours grief while worthlessness and guilt favour depression
Fleeting perceptions of the deceased are common and not psychotic
Prolonged grief disorder requires impairment beyond six to twelve months
explanation.pearls: Active suicidal ideation with a wish to die rather than a passive wish to be with the deceased is the feature that should move a bereaved patient out of the grief category and into treatment for depression, irrespective of how recent the loss was.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a reduced ratio on spirometry performed without a bronchodilator in a lifelong smoker
stem:
A 58 year old woman attends your practice with three years of breathlessness on exertion and a morning cough. She has smoked fifteen cigarettes daily since her twenties.

She has had two chest infections in the past year, each treated with antibiotics. She reports that her breathlessness varies considerably, being worse on some days than others, and that she wakes occasionally at night with chest tightness. Her practice nurse performed spirometry this morning without administering a bronchodilator first. Her chest radiograph shows no focal abnormality and no hyperinflation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Scattered expiratory wheeze, no crackles, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Forced expiratory volume in one second 1.72 L at 64 per cent predicted, forced vital capacity 2.80 L, ratio 0.61, no bronchodilator given, chest radiograph unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and commence a long acting bronchodilator now
options.rationale: Committing to a lifelong diagnosis on a pre-bronchodilator measurement risks mislabelling reversible disease that would be managed differently. The confirmatory test has not yet been done. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X

options.text: Diagnose asthma and commence an inhaled corticosteroid with a long acting bronchodilator now
options.rationale: Variable symptoms and nocturnal waking raise this possibility but it equally requires objective confirmation of variable airflow limitation. Treating on symptoms alone leaves the diagnosis unestablished. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Repeat the spirometry after a bronchodilator to establish whether the obstruction persists
options.rationale: A diagnosis of fixed airflow obstruction requires a ratio below 0.7 that persists after bronchodilator, and a pre-bronchodilator measurement cannot distinguish it from reversible obstruction. Her variable symptoms and nocturnal waking make that distinction clinically important. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest to assess for emphysema before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Diagnosis rests on physiology demonstrated by spirometry rather than on structural imaging, and computed tomography adds radiation without resolving the question. It is reserved for suspected bronchiectasis, nodules or surgical assessment. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X

options.text: Measure the transfer factor for carbon monoxide before making any diagnosis or starting treatment
options.rationale: Gas transfer helps characterise emphysema and interstitial disease but is not the test that establishes airflow obstruction. The immediate question is whether the obstruction reverses. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X

explanation.summary: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is defined physiologically by airflow obstruction that is not fully reversible, and the diagnosis therefore cannot be made without post-bronchodilator spirometry. A ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity below 0.7 measured after a bronchodilator establishes persistent obstruction, while a pre-bronchodilator measurement alone cannot separate this from asthma or from a transient effect of a recent infection. The distinction matters because management diverges sharply, with inhaled corticosteroids central in asthma and used more selectively in chronic obstructive disease, and because a mistaken lifelong label carries implications for insurance and employment. Some patients have features of both conditions, with a smoking history, fixed obstruction, variable symptoms and eosinophilia, and are managed with attention to both components. Severity is graded by the post-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume as a percentage of predicted, but symptom burden and exacerbation frequency drive treatment escalation more than the number alone.
key_points: The diagnosis requires post-bronchodilator spirometry showing a ratio below 0.7
Pre-bronchodilator measurement cannot separate fixed from reversible obstruction
Management diverges sharply between asthma and fixed obstruction
Some patients show features of both and need attention to each component
Symptoms and exacerbations drive escalation more than the percentage predicted
explanation.pearls: Spirometry performed during or shortly after a chest infection can show obstruction that resolves completely, so confirmatory testing is deferred until the patient has been stable for at least six weeks.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia and Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: COPD-X
National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

subtopic_detail: Dosing decision for a glycopeptide antibiotic on day four when the creatinine has risen and the next dose is due
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 73 year old man on day four of intravenous vancomycin for a methicillin resistant staphylococcal bacteraemia arising from an infected dialysis catheter that has since been removed.

He has improved clinically, is afebrile and his repeat blood cultures are negative. He also received two days of gentamicin on admission before the organism was identified. His creatinine was 88 micromol/L on admission and is 176 micromol/L today, with a urine output of 0.6 mL/kg/h over the past twelve hours. His next vancomycin dose is due in one hour and the nursing staff ask whether to give it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Catheter exit site clean after removal, no new murmur, no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 176 micromol/L rising from 88 on admission, urine output 0.6 mL/kg/h over twelve hours, repeat blood cultures negative, last vancomycin level not yet taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action regarding the next dose?

options.text: Give the dose as charted and measure a level before the dose that follows it tomorrow
options.rationale: Administering a further dose into a rising creatinine without a level risks substantial accumulation and worsening renal injury. The level is needed before rather than after the next administration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give half the charted dose now and continue at that reduced dose without measuring a level
options.rationale: Empirical dose halving without measurement may still accumulate or, alternatively, produce subtherapeutic concentrations in a bacteraemia where adequate exposure matters. Guesswork is unnecessary when an assay is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Cease the vancomycin entirely and switch to oral antibiotic therapy to complete the course
options.rationale: Staphylococcal bacteraemia requires a defined course of intravenous therapy, and oral substitution at this stage risks relapse and deep seated complications. The problem is dosing rather than the agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Withhold the dose and measure a level now, redosing according to the result and renal function
options.rationale: Vancomycin is renally cleared and accumulates as filtration falls, so giving a further dose before knowing the concentration risks compounding the nephrotoxicity that is already evident. Measuring before redosing allows the interval and dose to be set against the actual concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give the dose as charted and commence intravenous fluid to protect renal function overnight
options.rationale: Fluid may help if he is volume deplete but does not prevent accumulation of a drug that is already not being cleared. It addresses one contributor while continuing the other. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Vancomycin requires therapeutic drug monitoring because it is almost entirely renally cleared, has a narrow window between effective and toxic exposure, and is itself nephrotoxic, particularly when combined with other nephrotoxins such as aminoglycosides. The clinical trap in this case is that a patient can be improving from the infection while deteriorating from the treatment, so clinical response offers no reassurance about drug handling. When renal function changes, the correct sequence is to withhold the next dose, measure a concentration, and then redose according to that result rather than to the original schedule, because the elimination half life lengthens as filtration falls and the usual interval no longer applies. Australian practice increasingly favours area under the curve guided dosing over trough concentrations alone, since it correlates better with both efficacy and nephrotoxicity. Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia additionally requires source control, repeat blood cultures to confirm clearance, consideration of echocardiography to exclude endocarditis, and a defined duration of intravenous therapy.
key_points: Vancomycin is renally cleared and is itself nephrotoxic
Concurrent aminoglycoside exposure compounds the renal risk
Clinical improvement gives no reassurance about drug accumulation
Withhold and measure before redosing when renal function changes
Staphylococcal bacteraemia needs source control and repeat cultures
explanation.pearls: In Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia, repeat blood cultures at 48 to 72 hours are what define persistent infection and prompt a search for endocarditis or a deep focus, and they are taken regardless of how well the patient looks.
